key_claims: Scopolamine administration disrupted hippocampal slow theta oscillations (2–4 Hz) during both memory encoding and retrieval.
Presence of scopolamine during encoding impaired recollection-based memory performance.
Presence of scopolamine during retrieval disrupted slow theta oscillations without impairing memory performance.
Scopolamine caused dose-dependent reductions in hippocampal theta power, theta phase reset, and encoding–retrieval pattern reinstatement.
limitations: The research was conducted in a specific clinical population of neurosurgical patients with intracranial electrodes.
The study focused on scopolamine, a muscarinic cholinergic antagonist, which may not capture all aspects of cholinergic signaling or therapeutic interventions.
Clinical efficacy of specific therapies targeting these rhythmic biomarkers was not directly evaluated.
what_not_to_say: Do not claim that theta oscillations are strictly required for memory retrieval.
Do not claim that scopolamine causes permanent memory loss or cures Alzheimer's disease.
Do not extrapolate these neurophysiological findings to botanical, joint, enzymatic, mucosal, or blood DNA methylation clock outcomes not measured in the source.
